title: Interaction driven charge transfer transitions in closely spaced graphene double layers
authors: Kenneth A. Lin, Unmesh Ghorai, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Emanuel Tutuc, Rafi Bistritzer
abstract: Charge transfer between two conductors is conventionally viewed as a single-particle process governed by electrostatics and band alignment. Using tunneling spectroscopy, we show that charge transfer in closely spaced graphene double layer quantum Hall ferromagnets instead proceeds through a sequence of interaction driven phase transitions governed by the competition between capacitive charging and Coulomb exchange interactions. A comparison of experimental data and theoretical calculations identifies spectroscopic signatures of the interaction driven charge transfer transitions, and reveals that this charge transfer reconstructs the quasiparticle spectrum. While intralayer exchange favors abrupt transfer of entire spin-valley subbands between the layers, interlayer exchange stabilizes coherent intermediate phases that enable gradual charge transfer. Our results establish interlayer tunneling as a powerful probe of interacting electronic systems whose quasiparticle spectrum is itself bias dependent.
summary: This work demonstrates that charge transfer in closely spaced graphene double layers is a complex many-body process driven by the interplay between capacitive charging and various exchange interactions. By analyzing tunneling spectroscopy, the authors identify spectroscopic signatures corresponding to phase transitions where interlayer coherence allows for gradual, rather than abrupt, electronic rearrangement. This establishes interlayer tunneling as a sensitive probe of interacting quantum systems.
main_problem: The study investigates how charge transfer occurs in closely spaced graphene double layers, arguing that it is governed by interaction-driven phase transitions rather than simple single-particle physics.
main_result: Interlayer tunneling reveals a competition between capacitive charging and exchange interactions; specifically, interlayer exchange stabilizes coherent intermediate phases enabling gradual charge transfer, while intralayer exchange favors abrupt polarization.
method: The authors combine theoretical minimization of an effective Hamiltonian (Hartree-Fock approximation) with the analysis of experimental tunneling spectroscopy data ($dI/dV$).
model_or_system: The system is a closely spaced graphene double layer quantum Hall ferromagnet. The physics is modeled by minimizing an energy functional that includes terms for electrostatic charging, intralayer exchange ($\Gamma_A$), and interlayer exchange ($\Gamma_m^2$).
key_observables: Tunneling conductance ($g_{Int}$) as a function of interlayer bias ($V_{Int}$), which exhibits non-monotonic behavior marking phase transitions.
important_parameters: Interlayer separation ($d \approx 1.8$ nm); the competition between charging, intralayer exchange, and interlayer exchange energies; applied interlayer bias ($V_{Int}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Hartree-Fock approximation for determining ground state occupations and uses a perturbative approach for calculating tunneling current in coherent sectors.
figures_summary: Figures show $g_{Int}$ vs. gate voltages indicating LL filling oscillations, and critically, non-monotonic kinks in $I_{Int}/g_{Int}$ vs. $V_{Int}$ at $	ext{V}_{Int} \approx \pm 20 	ext{ mV}$, which signal the interaction-driven transitions.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework by defining the energy functional based on competing interactions, analyzes the ground state evolution through different bias regimes (coherent vs. polarized), and uses this theory to interpret spectroscopic signatures observed in tunneling measurements.
why_interesting: The concept of charge transfer being mediated by coherent intermediate phases stabilized by interlayer exchange is highly relevant for understanding correlated electron behavior in nanoscale heterostructures, bridging concepts from quantum optics/open systems into solid-state physics.

Temperature dependence of the tunneling characteristics. a–b, Measured IInt and gInt versus VInt at B = 12 T for temperatures between T = 1.5 K and 100 K. c, Peak heights of the symmetric conductance features marked by the gray and red arrows in b. As the temperature increases, the sharp conductance peaks associated with the charge transfer transitions broaden and gradually disappear. The persistence of these tunneling signatures to temperatures of several tens of kelvin reflects the large interaction energy scales driving the charge transfer transitions.
